messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Meera is a thirty-year-old software engineer who grew up in a close-knit South Asian family in the suburbs of Chicago. When she was eight years old, her father, a man who drank heavily on weekends, would come home late and find fault with everything. One particular night, after a family gathering where the adults had been drinking, he accused her of spilling food on the carpet, though she hadn’t. She remembered the sharp, sour smell of alcohol on his breath as he leaned over her, the acrid, salty taste of her own tears and sweat as she tried to explain, and the overwhelming scent of his body odor as he grabbed her arm and hit her across the back of her head. She had been too stunned to cry out, and the sequence of that night has always felt jumbled—she cannot be sure if the shouting came before the slap, or if the smell of the spilled food came before the smell of him, but the sensations themselves have never faded.

Now, at thirty, Meera works from home as a developer, a job that usually offers her a sense of control. But the world has become a minefield of unexpected intrusions. A few weeks ago, her husband came home from the gym and kissed her cheek; the faint, warm smell of his sweat immediately triggered a wave of nausea and a racing heart. In that moment, the memory of her father’s body odor crashed over her, leaving her breathless and unable to concentrate for the rest of the evening. She finds that these olfactory triggers—the smell of alcohol on a neighbor’s breath in the elevator, the taste of a particular spice that reminds her of that night’s dinner—do not just bring the memory back; they bring the whole feeling of helplessness with them. Because these triggers are so unpredictable, she has begun to feel that no place is truly safe, and she cannot relax even when she knows she is logically secure. She has taken to checking the locks on her doors and windows three times before bed, and she often lies awake for hours, her mind looping back to that confused, fragmented memory, as if trying to solve a puzzle that has no solution.

The more her memory intrudes, the more she feels overwhelmed by the raw emotion of it, and she has developed a habit of pushing the thought away before it can fully form. But this blocking has its own cost: the memory feels even more chaotic and powerful when it does return, and the threat of its arrival makes her hypervigilant. She has started avoiding cooking certain dishes that might carry that vague, triggering taste, and she will not sit next to anyone who smells of alcohol at a restaurant. Her husband has noticed her flinching when he hugs her after a long day, and she has stopped going to weekend barbecues with his family, inventing excuses about work deadlines. The occupational cost is mounting; she has trouble concentrating on code reviews because her brain is constantly scanning for smells, and she has fallen behind on two projects. What finally brought her to seek help was the exhaustion of this cycle: the way a single taste or smell can hijack her entire nervous system, the way the memory feels both too close and too jumbled, and the growing fear that she is losing her grip on the safe, stable life she has worked so hard to build. She is most afraid that she will never be able to trust her own senses again—that the world will always smell like that night.
